title: He Who Learns Teaches
subtitle: Knowledge Grows When It Is Shared With Others
author: Babi Magil
summary: This proverb teaches that true knowledge is not complete when it is only kept by one person. A person who learns has a responsibility to share that knowledge and help others grow.

sections.heading: The Proverb
content: “He who learns teaches.”

sections.heading: Origin & History
content: This proverb reflects a widespread African oral tradition and does not have a confirmed single ethnic owner.

Across many African communities, knowledge was preserved through elders, storytellers, skilled workers, hunters, farmers, and community leaders who passed their understanding from one generation to another.

sections.heading: Meaning
content: The proverb teaches that learning creates responsibility. When someone gains knowledge, they should use it to benefit others.
Knowledge becomes more valuable when it is shared. A person who learns a skill but refuses to teach others allows that knowledge to disappear.
The greatest teachers are often people who first became students themselves.

sections.heading: Cultural Significance
content: Traditional African societies depended on the transfer of knowledge between generations. Elders taught young people about history, survival skills, leadership, farming, traditions, and values.
A person was respected not only for what they knew but also for their willingness to guide others.

sections.heading: Story
content: In a small village, there lived an old farmer named Maku who knew how to grow crops even during difficult seasons.
For many years, young farmers came to him asking how he produced healthy harvests while others struggled.
One young man asked, 'Grandfather, why do you always share your secrets? Would you not become less special if everyone learned your skills?'
Maku smiled and answered, 'A tree does not lose its fruit because it feeds others. Knowledge is the same. It grows when it is shared.'
The young farmers learned from him and improved their farming methods. Soon, the entire village had better harvests.
Years later, Maku became old and could no longer work in the fields. However, his knowledge continued through the farmers he had taught.
The elders said, 'A person who learns but does not teach carries knowledge to the grave. A person who teaches allows wisdom to live forever.'

sections.heading: Life Lessons
content: Knowledge should be shared.
Learning creates responsibility.
Teaching others keeps wisdom alive.
A good teacher creates future generations of learners.
Helping others grow is a form of leadership.

sections.heading: Modern Application
content: This proverb applies to education, technology, business, and personal development. Professionals, teachers, and leaders create greater impact when they train and support others.
In the digital age, sharing knowledge through books, videos, and online platforms allows wisdom to reach more people.
